title: The cycle (Judges 2:11–19)
hookLine: the people stray, suffer, cry out, and a judge rescues them, again and again

lines: WASH, RINSE, SPIN, AND ROUND AGAIN.
A GENERATION WHICH KNEW NOT THE LORD.
cards: A washing machine has a dial. Wash, rinse, spin, and round again to the start. The book of Judges has one too, and it shows it to you before the first story.
Joshua is gone. His generation is gone. And the text says plainly that another generation arose after them, "which knew not the LORD."
Nobody rebels in a single dramatic moment. People forget. And from that forgetting, the book sets its dial turning, and it keeps turning for chapter after chapter.

teach.b: Chapter two lays out the whole pattern in a few verses, like a summary on the back of a book. First, the people stray: they serve the gods of the land and forsake the Lord who brought them out of Egypt.
Second, they suffer: they're handed over to raiders and enemies, and greatly distressed. Third, they cry out; the passage calls it their groaning.

teach.h: A SHOFET IS RAISED UP AND SAVES.
teach.b: Fourth, the Lord raises up a shofet, and the shofet saves them. Then the turn: when the shofet dies, they go back and do worse than their fathers. And the dial comes round again.
Shofet is usually translated judge, and the book is called Shoftim, Judges. But in this book a shofet is mostly not someone in a courtroom.

The text says the Lord raised up judges who delivered them out of the hand of those who plundered them. A shofet is a rescuer, raised up in a crisis, who leads while they live. Two details are worth slowing down for.
Why does God send a rescuer? The text doesn't say the people repented.
It says the Lord was moved by their groaning, because of those who oppressed and crushed them. The help comes in answer to pain, before anyone has changed. And the cycle isn't a perfect circle.
When each judge dies, the people turn back and act more corruptly than their fathers.

teach.h: EACH TIME ROUND, A LITTLE LOWER.
teach.b: Each time round, a little lower. It's a pattern you can watch, and name, and once you see it, recognize in other places.

how: Jews read Judges, Shoftim, among the Former Prophets, right after Joshua; its chapter two sets out the pattern of straying, oppression, crying out and rescue that the later stories follow.

o: a rescuer raised up in a crisis, called a judge
a court officer who records the people's laws
a prophet who warns before the enemies come

games.q: the cycle repeats — tap the pairs.
p: serve the gods of the land

s: in the book of Judges, a judge mainly runs a courtroom
the text says the Lord raised up judges who delivered them: rescuers and leaders in a crisis.
the text says God sent help because the people repented
it says the Lord was moved by their groaning under those who oppressed them.
after each judge died, the people went back to their old ways
and, the text says, did worse than their fathers.

games.q: you're a shofet. you've rescued your people, and there's peace. you know the pattern. what happens when you die?
o: the people go back, and do worse.
your children lead in your place.
games.why: when the judge died, the text says, they turned back and dealt more corruptly than their fathers. the dial comes round again.

practice: Let one pattern of your own come to mind, small is fine: the late night that leads to the bad morning, the argument that always starts the same way, the promise to yourself that fades by the weekend.
Walk it through its stages the way chapter two does: where it starts, where the forgetting is, where it hurts, what you do when it does. Don't fix it now; just see the dial.
